# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies to watch for Film Analysis class

**Score:** 63
**Body:** I’m looking for about 20 movies but 10 I have to pick for my film analysis class in high school. I’m not a movie person and would actually like to start watching movies.

It says that I should have a movie that’s critically acclaimed and just a movie but both movies should “portray human struggles in a sense” and one of the movies should be more than 20 years old at least one of them.

Any help is appreciated.

(Edit) Its 2 movies that portray human struggle, 2 movies that challenge existing culture, 2 movies that tackle current events, 2 movies that create icons and stars, and 2 movies that broke records.

I've checked on some of these movies and they seem pretty good even if I might not use these I'll still have to check them out sometime. Thanks guys!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Little Miss Sunshine (2006) - Every character is struggling. It's a great watch.
2. A usual suggestion, but Bicycle Thieves is a fantastic movie to analyze the human struggle. It shows you how pure desperation corrupts personal morality in a broken system. It seems like the usual film school answer, but this one was truly incredible. 
3. I have some recs on the classic side. Top rec is Some Like it Hot. It's funny but subversive, the script is phenomenal, and it's directed by Billy Wilder. If you want something dark, Night of the Hunter is absolutely incredible. Directed by Charles Laughton. For action and suspense, along with great pacing and shots, check out North by  northwest or To Catch a Thief by Alfred Hitchcock. 
4. O Brother Where Art Thou. 2 of my professors used that film as an example of This Is An Excellent Movie when I was studying film at uni. 
5. What's Eating Gilbert Grape
6. Rear Window and/or Rope
7. Amadeus 
8. Pulp Fiction 
9. Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf
10. It Happened One Night - critically acclaimed, often on best movie lists, is over 80 years old, legendary actors, and because it was made during the depression there’s an ongoing theme of people struggling.   
My Man Godfrey was made around the same time and checks the same boxes

## 4. My review of ( The lure (2015) starring Michalina Olszańska and Marta Mazurek

**Body:** What up y'all!!Hope y'all are doing well😌.It is day 20 ( Oct 20 th ) of watching a Horror movie (or two or three, Maybe four idk )every night until Halloween. I will say I skipped a day or two ( actually more like 3 ) but I had great reasoning. I went to the ER a day or two ago because I had been feeling absolutely horrible for a day or two ( constant migraine and nausea, I was hungry but I couldn't eat, my stomach hurt, and I kinda felt like I was dying ngl ) turns out I just had one of the worst stomach bugs I've ever had but I got medicine and started feeling a little better yesterday but still didn't feel like doing too much. I am happy to say I finally feel good enough to be able to watch a movie tonight so that's fun for me and fun for y'all cuz y'all get a review lol( I will try to catch up but I'm going to take my time and not watch four movies in one night lol).

Today I watched The lure (2015) which is a movie i've been wanting to watch for a long time but haven't got to because I've been busy and it was one of the first movies I had on my list for movies to watch in October. I had heard of it from a YouTuber( Da\\\_Narrator go check his stuff out he does movie reviews )but what really got me wanting to watch was that it was a horror comedy musical!?! (I love horror comedy musicals nerdy erdy prudes must die is my favorite if anyone wanted to know lol). Which for a movie I feel is a pretty unique genre (I could be wrong. If y'all know of anymore please let me know. I would love to watch more horror comedy musical movies I know the demon barber of fleet Street Starring Johnny Depp I believe is one but I don't know many others other than that one.) It was nothing like I expected but it was a fun movie!.

Little synopsis:

Two mermaid sisters are helped onto land , both fascinated in humans, one for love, and the other for hunger.

Genre: musical horror comedy

Rating: 7.5/10

Where I watched: Tubi

What I liked about this movie:

\\- It was very unique

\\- the characters were done well

\\- I liked that there were minor gay relationships that weren't like a huge thing (as a queer person 🖤🩶🤍,💜🩷💜💙It was cool to see a gay relationship just in the background every now and then in this movie)

\\- The special effects were pretty cool

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Movies about life and/or passage of time

**Score:** 33
**Body:** I am looking for movies about life and/or the passage of time- not time travelling, but instead the melancholy, the bittersweet nostalgia of the days passing, brevity of life and the impermanence of things. Topics like how your life decisions impact or alter the course of life, maybe regrets can be part of it too. I think there is a Japanese word for it- mono no aware.

Any recommendations would be appreciated.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The obvious answer here is Kurosawa’s masterpiece Ikiru, which is about a Tokyo bureaucrat whose cancer diagnosis sends him on a Scrooge-esque journey into whether his life had any meaning and what his passing would mean for others. A beautiful, bittersweet, unmissable film. And for something more modern, Kore-eda’s film After Life, which approaches this same theme in a completely different way. Both are life-changing and profound films, but quiet and subtle. 
  - Yes I have watched After Life, quite a thought-provoking movie! 
2. A River Runs Through It (1992)

Legends of the Fall (1994)

About Time (2013) is about time travel, but it hits the melancholy note about the passage of time perfectly. 

Train Dreams (2025)

Cesar et Rosalie (1972)

La Strada (1954)

Amarcord (1973)

Cinema Paradiso (1988)
  - Train Dreams nails this. Such a great movie. That scene where he’s looking at the tv 😭
3. I hugely recommend the Up series of documentaries by Michael Apted. It started in 1964 with Seven Up, following 12 children aged 7, their hopes, perspectives on things. Then revisited them aged 14, then every seven years to age 70 (the final episode, which aired last month). I binge watched them all a couple of weeks ago and it was an absolutely mind-blowing experience. There is nothing else like it. They all contain appropriate flashbacks to prior ages, so you could just watch the last one. The various trajectories are quite astonishing. 
  - Wow and I thought Richard Linklater’s “Boyhood” spanned a lot of time. 
4. I'd say most of Terence Malick's works have that feeling.

Also, Boyhood offers a more literal and explicit depiction of the passage of time.  
Some of Kurosawa's films have that feeling
5. There's a recent Japanese film called Perfect Days that hits on some of the themes you described. The director, Wim Wenders, has a filmography you might want to look into. He explores life choices and their results often.
6. As I Was Moving Ahead Occasionally I Saw Brief Glimpses of Beauty (2000)

Wild Strawberries (1957)

World of Tomorrow (2015) (and its sequels; technically there's time travel, but the focus is on memory and the impermanence of things)

La Jetée (1962) (also has time travel, but only in service of the themes you mentioned)

The Beaches of Agnès (2008)

Sans Soleil (1983)

The Long Day Closes (1992) (though this one is just about a young boy, the whole thing feels like a bittersweet, nostalgic look back on the impermanence of childhood)
7. Yi Yi by Edward Yang is perfect for this. It’s a story of a year of life for a Taiwanese family, starting with a wedding and ending with a funeral. It focuses on all the family members from a seven-year-old boy to 70+ year-old grandma, and all the stages of life are kind of played out in them. A lot of it has to do with regrets and choices in youth, wondering how life could have been different, and seeing the echoes of the older generation playing out in younger. It’s absolute cinema perfection and I can’t recommend it highly enough if you are looking for films about life and time.

I’d also echo the recommendation for Ikiru, which is my 2nd favourite film!

## 2. For anyone familiar with American International Pictures (AIP): how do you feel about the studio and its legacy?

**Score:** 11
**Body:** I’m especially curious if you know about its scrappy, low-budget identity and the way it built movies around youth culture, genre films, campy and serious horror, and exploitation-era marketing. Do you see AIP as an important, inventive studio? Do you enjoy the old movies about girls, cars, juvenile delinquency, the horror movies etc.?

These days, those movies are kinda relegated to Turner Classic Movies. Some films are regarded as classics. Others are forgotten.  

I think Samuel Arkoff helped build AIP into a major force in low-budget genre filmmaking, with a knack for spotting what young audiences might want and marketing films on a shoestring. 

Thoughts?



### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. AIP and Roger Corman did a lot for fostering this independent, guerilla-style filmmaking that eventually brought the New Hollywood era. Corman gave a start to a lot of young actors and filmmakers, including Francis Ford Coppola, Peter Bogdanovich, Jack Nicholson etc
  - Yeah.

It does have a very important legacy in American film history. 
2. AIP gave so many directors their start which is pretty crazy. Like Corman alone launched Coppola, Scorsese, etc. The actual movies are hit or miss but their impact on Hollywood is hard to deny
3. AIP made a lot of crap, but a good amount of it is FUN. 

Their importing of foreign films, like horror and Godzilla films, which they subsequently re-dubbed (and often hacked in editing) is legendary. 

But their biggest gift was Roger Corman. When Corman told them he could take the low budgets of two black and white films and use it to make one low budget color film that would make them MORE money, and they reluctantly agreed, we got the Poe Cycle, most of them starring Vincent Price. Those films still hold up just because of Prices acting and Corman's direction. Even with the low budget they had atmosphere and style.
4. Slow to respond to this thread, but I bring gifts

I enjoy AIP films and while they are seen as largely exploitation/genre pictures, they are varied as you stated and important overall to film and film discourse. Without AIP you don't get a lot of New Hollywood (Coppola, Scorsese, Bogdanovich, to name a few), you don't get Tarantino later…the list is almost endless.

The[ wiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_International_Pictures) is fascinating due to the ARKOFF formula and the Peter Pan Syndrome -

*Samuel Z. Arkoff related his "ARKOFF formula" for producing a successful low-budget movie years later, during a 1980s talk show appearance. His ideas for a movie included:*

***A****ction (exciting, entertaining drama)*

***R****evolution (novel or controversial themes and ideas)*

***K****illing (a modicum of violence)*

***O****ratory (notable dialogue and speeches)*

***F****antasy (acted-out fantasies common to the audience)*

***F****ornication (sex appeal for young adults)*  
*Later, the AIP publicity department devised a strategy called "the Peter Pan Syndrome":*

*a) a younger child will watch anything an older child will watch;*  
*b) an older child will not watch anything a younger child will watch;*  
*c) a girl will watch anything a boy will watch;*  
*d) a boy will not watch anything a girl will watch;*  
*therefore:*  
*to catch your greatest audience you zero in on the 19-year-old male*

## 3. The movie Take Me to the River (2015)

**Score:** 6
**Body:** 
So I just watched Take Me to the River tonight. It wasn't what I was expecting because the genre said "thriller" so I thought something crazy would happen but nothing did. The whole movie is filmed in a way where, if you were to read what was happening on paper, you would read about interactions that seem pretty innocent, but from just a few scenes in onwards you get a really strong feeling of unease. The movie actually ended when I figured we were about halfway through and I was surprised to see the credits start rolling. 

I thought about it afterwards and thought I *mostly* understood what happened, except one thing. This was the ultimately revealed backstory of the movie to me: When Keith and Cindy were kids, they would hang out by the river, and Cindy would accidentally do sexual things while her brother was giving her a piggyback ride, and the mom blamed Keith, assuming he was molesting her. Decades later, Keith's daughter happens to do the same behavior (how did she learn to do that??? Happened to have the same quirk, just runs in the family?) and Keith gets revenge on Molly by falsely accusing her son, Ryder, and forcing her to live out the experience of being falsely accused by seeing it happen to her own son, and he even tagged their car with threats like what may have once happened to Keith. 

Then I looked at the decade old Reddit thread and they all seem to think that Keith is Ryder's biological father, that "chicken fighting" was a codeword for sex, and the reason Keith freaked out was that he assumed when the girl told him that she and Ryder were chicken fighting (it wasn't explicitly said to anyone other than Ryder) was that they'd had sex. I started to see it a little-- Keith teaches Ryder how to use a gun in a scene that seems like a red herring, but that's the kind of thing that a father would do with his son. The girl saying "they're not my real family" but then quickly taking it back also might allude to Ryder not really being his "father's " child, and apparently there was some "you're not really Jewish" line that I missed. 

I guess that's possible but I think what might have happened was that Keith trained his daughter to "chicken fight" and act in a way that implicates Ryder for assault. If he did that, he is a pervert, and maybe the accusations against him weren't wrong at all. 

It's hard to say. As a side note, I'm kind of horrified that they had an actual child actress do the chicken fighting scene. I don't think she could have fully understood what it was implied that she was doing when she was coached into that scene. 

I did enjoy it though because it was a movie that was all about atmosphere and personally I enjoy atmosphere over plot, but I am left wondering what happened exactly and where the blood in the initial scene came from. 

Did anyone else seen this?

Edit: also, I don't know if I'm stupid for this but for some reason I thought while watching it was that the implication was that the mom was trying to kill the brother by squeezing his neck so hard that he would pass out in the river 

Edit: I just realized something else that points to Keith really being a pervert. At the beginning, when Ryder is first being accused, Keith said, "I already checked her, no lacerations." The girl is obviously past the age that her father should be looking at her privates. I think the reason Ryder told his mom that she did nothing wrong at the end was because he realized based on the girl (Molly)'s behavior that the mom's accusations were actually true.

## 4. "The Devil Wears Prada 2" restyles the workplace comedy as "business comedy"

**Score:** 7
**Body:** Watching "The Devil Wears Prada 2" got me thinking about how the portrayal of working people in Hollywood movies, and pop culture in general, has changed over the years.

Looking far back, I can think of classics like "Modern Times" and "The Grapes of Wrath" addressing industrialization and unemployment, but I believe it was during the postwar period – let’s say, around the first peak of Marlon Brando’s career – that the ordinary wage earner who's defined by his work became a major protagonist.

Labor isn't at the center of "A Streetcar Named Desire", but Stanley’s brutality is rooted in working-class masculinity. In "On the Waterfront", Terry Malloy doesn’t just hold a job; he “belongs” to the longshoremen. When TV entered the picture, sitcoms about family life helped establish the idea of the dignified breadwinner who could support a home and family on a modest paycheck.

I think Sally Field’s character in "Norma Rae" is an interesting culmination of these trends. Her identity is tied to factory labor, and her victory comes not from escaping the working class but from demanding dignity within it. That movie came out in 1979, and I’d argue that the next economic and cinematic shift came right after Norma’s quest.

Because the workplace movies of the 1980s were less interested in celebrating the little American worker: their characters did not find (or *could* not find?) comfort in stability but went out into the world to climb the corporate ladder. By the time we got to “Working Girl”, that ladder was often in a glamorous skyscraper office, and this trend was still in vogue (no pun intended) when first “Devil" came about.

It was 2006. The image of the truly despicable corporate leader was still tied to the likes of Gordon Gekko in Oliver Stone’s “Wall Street”, and because Miranda Priestly was more of an asshole than a straightforwardly unscrupulous person, the original movie was not required to soften her. There was already a case to be made that Miranda took her work seriously and simply expected nothing but excellence from those around her.

I was prepared for the sequel to find more humanity in its devil because our social understanding of women in positions of power has changed, and so has everyday HR culture. But I naively thought this would be at the center of the story. Simply put, I expected another workplace comedy, only this time we’d watch Miranda having to put up with the “sensitivities” of her Gen-Z interns.

Well, there are some minor jokes about modern-day corporate etiquette: Miranda now has to hang up her own coats instead of throwing them at one of her assistants! But the core of the new movie is neither workplace dynamics nor the humanization of Miranda Priestly, though the character is indeed shown in a more positive and vulnerable light.

The core of this movie is corporate power. While the likes of “The Bear” and “Abbott Elementary” are here to prove that ordinary workers have not disappeared from fiction, their cultural relevance seems to have diminished in the era of celebrity CEOs and tech billionaires, who have dominated mainstream culture for years now.

From “Succession” to “Shark Tank”, we’ve grown comfortable with the image of the billionaire protagonist. Tony Stark, who made his Hollywood debut two years after the first "Devil" hit theaters, even added “genius,” “playboy” and “philanthropist” to the package. Watching someone climb the corporate ladder may no longer be as appealing, interesting or sexy as watching those who have already secured the top job or accumulated immense power and wealth.

I say all this because there are four different billionaire characters in the second “Devil”: the media mogul who owns Runway; this man’s son; the tech entrepreneur who might buy the conglomerate; and that man’s ex-wife. They are peripheral characters, but their presence shapes the entire plot: only their money can ensure the magazine’s survival, and the magazine can’t survive unless it keeps making them money.

The staff is under pressure not just to get Miranda’s steak delivered on time, but to get her the page views she needs to prove that Runway can remain financially viable in the digital age. That really threw me off the movie at first, but I get it: the sequel can’t give us the familiarity of returning home when the home itself has fundamentally changed, both in publishing and in Hollywood.

In the first movie, Miranda seemed to occupy the top of the hierarchy that mattered; twenty years later, Miranda's bosses are part of the picture; the workplace comedy hasn’t disappeared per se, but a new class of "business comedies" has emerged. Both the people who reached the top of the corporate ladder and the people who own the ladder are fashionable.

The movie itself is definitely not as fun or rewatchable as the original. But I can at least understand why they chose to go this way.
